Had you read about that story before you heard the broadcast, or were you coming to it cold?
I had read about it in Portuguese that morning. It was still too fast for me.
Too fast, or too much at once? Those are different problems and only one of them is about speed.
Too much at once, I think. I get the names and then I lose the sentence around them.
Then you are already doing the right thing. By the end of the year you will have listened to about two hundred of those reports, and by then the speed will have stopped being the problem.
And in the meantime? What should I be listening for?
The names and the days. They carry the skeleton, and while you are catching those you will be training the rest without noticing.
So I stop trying to hear the whole sentence and I start collecting the skeleton.

And that brings us to the week ahead. By Thursday the negotiators will have been in the same building for eleven days, which is longer than anybody expected and longer than either side wanted. The mediation has produced one thing so far, a truce that has held for six days, and by the weekend we will know whether it holds for a seventh. Watch the northern crossing on Tuesday. That is the flashpoint, and if the trucks are still waiting there on Wednesday morning the humanitarian side of this collapses before the political side does. Meanwhile, in Washington, the incumbent will be defending a record on foreign policy that half of his own party no longer supports, and by the time the electoral season starts in earnest, that record will have been rewritten at least twice.

If you want to follow the news in English by ear, stop trying to understand it the way you read it. Here is what actually works. First, know the story before you listen. Read two paragraphs about it in your own language, and you have just removed ninety percent of the difficulty, because you are no longer decoding the content and the language at the same time. Second, listen for the proper nouns. Names of people, names of places, days of the week. They are stressed, they are slow, and they are the skeleton of the report. Third, accept that you will miss the connecting words, and understand that this costs you almost nothing, because in a news report the connections are obvious once you have the skeleton. And fourth, listen to the same three minutes twice, on two different days. The second time will feel like a different recording, and that feeling is the only proof of progress you are going to get.
